transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-20
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Evan Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood Solutions), Laura Chen (CTO - Sierra), Diego Ruiz (Lead ML Eng - Sierra), Maya Singh (Head of Infra - Sierra), Tom Harper (PM - Sierra)
Shared artifacts: Deck: https://redwood.app/decks/sierra-poc-v1.pdf; Benchmark sheet: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/sierra-poc-bench.xlsx; Pilot config template: https://redwood.app/templates/pilot-config.md
Summary (auto): scoping for 2-week POC focused on unit economics and latency tradeoffs; customer has budget constraint for pilot ~ $15k/mo equivalent and needs 95th pct latency <250ms for web-facing conversational UI; next steps: Redwood to share cost model and bench plan, customer to provide workload traces.
Topics: success criteria, workload sizing, per-token estimates, batching & caching knobs, pilot timeline, concerned infra constraints (VPC, egress), benchmarking plan.

Transcript body:
[00:00:10] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for doing this — appreciate you carving time. Quick round if folks can intro?
[00:00:22] Laura: Hi, Laura here, CTO at Sierra. We're building a search+chat product for enterprise docs, low-latency, high-throughput.
[00:00:28] Diego: Diego, ML eng - I'll be driving benchmarks and the model pipeline.
[00:00:32] Maya: Maya, infra - I'll own networking and VPC questions.
[00:00:36] Tom: Tom, PM - focusing on success metrics, budgets.
[00:00:42] Priya: Priya from Redwood SE — I'll focus on perf and config recommendations.
[00:00:45] Evan: Great. Goal today: align on pilot success criteria, get rough workload numbers, and define what we bench. We'll also surface cost per token expectations and knobs.

[00:01:18] Evan: Laura, can you walk quick through expected qps, average prompt length, and where you serve from?
[00:01:26] Laura: Sure — baseline is a web chat, expect 200 concurrent users at peak, about 100 - 120 QPS read-ish? Sorry, um, our metric is 150-200 qps across global but initial pilot in us-west ~100 QPS. Average prompt size is 120 tokens in, response 220 tokens out. We also have some longer doc-summarize jobs ~2k tokens but those are rare.
[00:01:55] Diego: To add, our per-session pattern: short prompt -> quick followups; many short prefix repeats which we hoped to cache.
[00:02:05] Priya: Ok that's helpful. For cost modeling we'll split interactive small-turn traffic vs occasional long-run jobs. Caching can help a lot on the short prefix.

[00:02:50] Evan: On budget — Tom, you mentioned a pilot budget?
[00:02:54] Tom: Yep, we have about $15k/mo to validate performance and unit economics. We want to know if at scale production will be economically viable.
[00:03:03] Evan: Right. We'll size a 2-week bench to estimate per-token costs and extrapolate.

[00:03:45] Priya: Quick note on terminology — when I say batching I mean request-level batching into GPUs to reduce per-token overhead; caching refers to prefix/KV or embedding-level cache. They have different tradeoffs for latency.
[00:04:00] Maya: Side note: we need VPC peering and egress constraints — can Redwood run inside our VPC for the pilot?
[00:04:08] Evan: For pilot we can do a private deployment option (VPC peered) or a dedicated tenant with strict egress rules; we'll include that in the pilot config.

[00:04:45] Diego: What's a realistic per-token delta we should expect vs running open-source in-house? Our infra team thinks raw cost on baremetal is lower but ops/time is high.
[00:04:56] Priya: Good question. Ballpark: for similar model families, Redwood hosted runtime with batching + KV caching often gets effective per-token costs ~30-60% lower than naive single-request runs because of continuous batching and prefix caching. For example, a 2k-context smaller transformer might land ~ $0.0004 - $0.0009 per token effective in host env depending on requests/ batching. That's a wide range.
[00:05:25] Evan: Important to note—cost per token is very workload dependent: short-turn chat with high reuse = much cheaper; long generate jobs = higher. We'll surface both per-token and per-conversation costs.

[00:06:10] Laura: Our success criteria: (1) 95th pct latency <250ms for interactive flows, (2) per-1k-token cost below $0.35 for typical chat workloads, (3) no more than 5% error/regression compared to our baseline model for answer quality. Is that reasonable?
[00:06:25] Priya: Those are clear. The 95th pct under 250ms is aggressive but doable with proper batching limits and smaller context windows for interactive calls. We'll propose two config variants: latency-optimized (lower batching, more replicas) and cost-optimized (higher batching + caching).
[00:06:43] Tom: For quality measurement — Diego will provide a prompt set and correctness metrics, we want to make sure cost tuning doesn't degrade outputs.

[00:07:20] Priya: On benchmarks — we recommend a 2-week run with: 1) 48-hour synthetic microbench to map latency vs batch sizes, 2) 1-week production replay with your sample traffic, 3) final 3-day A/B comparing Redwood serving vs their current infra on cost/latency/quality. We'll collect token counts, latency histograms, P95/P99, and cache hit rates.
[00:07:46] Diego: That replay is doable — I'll anonymize traces. How do you want the traffic formatted?
[00:07:50] Priya: JSONL with timestamp, prompt, conversation_id, and expected metadata. We have a template in the shared artifacts.

[00:08:30] Evan: Let's get into concrete numbers for the cost model. Priya, do you have a worked example?
[00:08:34] Priya: Yup. Example scenario: 100 QPS, 120 tokens in / 220 tokens out average. That's ~34M tokens/day. Over 30 days ~1B tokens. If effective per-token cost is $0.0005 then monthly would be $500k — obviously huge. For pilot we scope 2 weeks at a smaller fraction. With caching and batching we might reduce effective tokens by 20-40% if there's prefix reuse. So for the pilot size (10% of projected production) you'd see maybe $25k-40k equivalent unless we optimize more.
[00:09:05] Laura: Wait, those numbers are higher than our $15k budget — can we get to $15k for the MVP?
[00:09:12] Priya: For the MVP, you can trade off latency and quality: using a smaller model variant for short-turn chat (or quantized model) and aggressive caching can push cost down. Example: using quantized medium model + cache hit 40% + batching yields effective per-token maybe $0.0002-$0.0003 — that would bring a pilot into the $15k range for limited traffic. But need real traces to validate.

[00:09:55] Maya: Are there additional fixed costs or reserved fees for dedicated capacity?
[00:09:59] Evan: For Dedicated you can do committed monthly capacity; there's a platform fee plus the compute reservation. We'll include a couple pricing scenarios: pure hosted pay-as-you-go vs 3-month dedicated commit. Often the dedicated route lowers unit costs if you sustain throughput.

[00:10:30] Diego: Regarding batching knobs — what's an optimal batch size for low-latency chat?
[00:10:35] Priya: For interactive RPS and SLOs like P95 <250ms, we keep batching small: batch size 4-8 with micro-batching window ~10-20ms. For highest throughput, batch size 16-32 works but adds tail latency. Redwood's runtime supports variable batching per route.
[00:11:00] Tom: And caching strategy?
[00:11:03] Priya: Implement LRU prefix cache at inference side plus KV cache for repeated document retrieval. If you have many repeated system prompts or boilerplate, hits can be 30-50% which materially reduces tokens. We'll instrument cache-hit metrics in the bench.

[00:11:40] Laura: On quality R? If we use quantized model are we likely to see regressions?
[00:11:46] Priya: Quantization can introduce small regressions; we'll run a quality regression test over your prompt set and flag any significant deltas. We'll recommend model variants that balance quality and quantization level.

[00:12:30] Samir: Ops question — for VPC, what's the deployment cadence? Is there a lead time for private deployments?
[00:12:35] Evan: Private VPC deployments usually are a 2-4 week setup depending on networking approvals. For pilot we can start with hosted but locked-down routes while parallelizing VPC setup.
[00:12:52] Maya: Ok that timing works. We'll start security review in parallel.

[00:13:30] Diego: Can Redwood provide a headroom plan — e.g., how to scale from 100 qps to 1k qps and expected unit cost improvements?
[00:13:36] Priya: Yep — we'll include a scaling curve in the cost model: expected unit cost reduction vs sustained qps and reserved GPU pools; typically you see 20-40% unit cost improvements at higher sustained throughput due to better batching and amortized kernel costs.

[00:14:15] Evan: Let's capture acceptance criteria for the POC now.
[00:14:20] Tom: Acceptances: P1 - 95th pct latency <250ms on interactive workload; P2 - per-1k-token cost below $0.35 for typical chat set; P3 - quality regression <5% on evaluation prompts; P4 - dashboarding + logs integrated with our SSO.
[00:14:36] Priya: We'll map those to bench checks and create a pass/fail rubric.

[00:15:10] Laura: Timeline? We want pilot results in 6 weeks ideally.
[00:15:15] Evan: Proposed timeline: this week: exchange traces & cost sheet. Week 1: bench infra + synthetic microbench (48h). Week 2: production replay (7 days). Week 3: A/B analysis & wrap — deliverables end of week 3 after bench begins; ~5 calendar weeks from now. We can compress if needed.
[00:15:37] Diego: That works if we get the artifacts quickly.

[00:16:20] Priya: Technical bench plan details: we'll collect token-level telemetry, per-request latency, batch size distribution, GPU occupancy, cache hit rates, and memory usage. We'll also run stress test to P99 to see tail behavior.
[00:16:42] Maya: For profiling GPU: we'll need to allow some monitoring endpoints; are you able to redact anything sensitive?
[00:16:48] Priya: Yes we'll keep logs token-less and you can share sanitized traces. We'll run with sample IDs not raw PII.

[00:17:30] Evan: Pricing scenarios to include in the spreadsheet: pay-as-you-go hosted; 1-month dedicated reserve; and a committed 3-month discount. Also show sensitivity analysis for cache hit rates (0%, 25%, 50%).
[00:17:50] Tom: Good — the sensitivity analysis will guide our internal stakeholders.

[00:18:20] Diego: What about fallbacks — if Redwood capacity spikes, how do we keep the app online?
[00:18:24] Priya: We can configure automatic fallback routes: lower-cost model variant, reduced max tokens, or degrade to cached responses. Redwood's routing policies allow region/model fallback with graceful degradation. We'll include that in the runbook.

[00:19:05] Laura: Any compliance hurdles — we need SOC2 and audit logs.
[00:19:09] Evan: Redwood has SOC2 and supports audit logs and KMS integrations for key management. We'll attach the security pack with the next email.

[00:19:40] Samir: For the bench data — do you need embeddings counts separately?
[00:19:44] Priya: Yes, embeddings are billed differently; please call out how many embedding calls and average dims. If you use embeddings for retrieval, that will change the econ.

[00:20:12] Diego: We do about 30k embedding calls/day at 1536 dims.
[00:20:18] Priya: Noted — we'll add embeddings to the cost sheet.

[00:21:00] Tom: One risk we're worried about is opaque token billing — can the bench produce a token-level ledger we can audit?
[00:21:05] Evan: Yes — our bench will output token-level accounting CSV per request with hashing of prompts. We'll include a sample ledger.

[00:21:40] Priya: Quick demo note — if we see long tail latency on large context calls, we may offload those to a background worker for async responses to avoid client-facing P95 spikes.
[00:21:55] Diego: Makes sense. We'll identify which flows are async-friendly.

[00:22:30] Laura: Ok so to recap — Redwood sends cost model, bench plan, security pack by Friday; we send sample traces and prompt sets by Sunday; schedule SE deep-dive for next week.
[00:22:42] Evan: Yep — that's the plan. Anything else?
[00:22:50] Maya: One more ask — can you include an example pilot config with explicit batching and cache params so our infra can sanity check ports/traffic?
[00:22:58] Priya: Absolutely — we'll attach pilot-config and default knobs: batch_window_ms=15, max_batch=8, prefix_cache_ttl=300s, kv_cache_size=100k, cache_eviction=LRU.
[00:23:18] Tom: Nice. Also can you add cost sensitivity for using quantized vs full fp16?
[00:23:22] Priya: Yep — we'll add columns for fp16, int8, and quant-llm variants.

[00:24:00] Evan: Great. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the deep dive and the pilot kickoff.
[00:24:08] Laura: Thanks all.
[00:24:12] Diego: Thanks.

[00:24:30] (call winds down, some small talk)
[00:25:10] Speaker 1: --
[00:26:00] [end excerpt — remainder is short wrap & scheduling]

Notes on transcription: transcription contains occasional mis-hears — e.g., quantization names sometimes transcribed as 'quanti-sation'. Some speaker labels may be generic.

Final recap (manual):
- Success criteria: P95 latency <250ms; cost per-1k tokens < $0.35 on typical chat; quality regressions <5%; logging and SSO integration.
- Pilot scope: 2-week benchmark consisting of 48h microbench, 7-day production replay, 3-day A/B.
- Budget/expectation: customer target ~$15k/mo pilot-equivalent; Redwood believes with caching+quantization can approach pilot target but needs real traces to validate.
- Deliverables: cost model spreadsheet, bench plan, security pack, pilot-config knobs.

Links again: cost model template: https://redwood.app/templates/cost-model-v2.xlsx; pilot config: https://redwood.app/templates/pilot-config.md; security pack: https://redwood.app/security/sierra-pack.zip
